By the end of this lab you should have: (1) a working LEAP JupyterHub login, (2) a GitHub account with a private course repository shared with the teaching staff, and (3) one completed notebook pushed to that repository and submitted on Courseworks.

## Part A — Accounts 

1. **GitHub.** If you don't have an account, create one at [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup). Use a professional-ish username (it may end up on your CV — some of you may link to course projects later). 
2. **JupyterHub (LEAP hub).** Most of our modeling and data analysis for this class will be done on the [LEAP computing hub](https://leap.2i2c.cloud/). To get access, **fill out this form now** (approval takes a little time — hope you did not leave it for today): [hub access request form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf_-vvkU__-rnaQimXRxAN_xGdQlqLulbBUistmetrhQtTjHg/viewform). 
   - When filling the form: pick the **Education tier**, enter **Dhruv Balwada** as primary contact, and use the same email/GitHub username as your course accounts (you need a GitHub account first — see step 1). 
   - **Already have LEAP hub access from a previous class? Skip the form** — just confirm you can still log in and access resources at [leap.2i2c.cloud](https://leap.2i2c.cloud/). 
   - Once approved, log in at **[leap.2i2c.cloud](https://leap.2i2c.cloud/)** and confirm your server starts (click "Start My Server" and wait for JupyterLab to load).

> **If the hub won't start for you:** discuss with Sarika or the TAs.

## Part C — Create your course repository 

1. On GitHub, click **New repository**:
   - Name: `climate-modeling-f26-<your-uni>` (e.g., `climate-modeling-f26-ab1234`)
   - Visibility: **Private** ← important
   - Check "Add a README file"
2. Add the teaching staff as collaborators: repo **Settings → Collaborators → Add people** — add **`dhruvbalwada`**, **`[PRANI-GITHUB]`**, and **`[CHANDANIE-GITHUB]`**.
3. **Make a personal access token** (needed for options 2 and 3 below; skip if you only do option 1). When git on the hub talks to GitHub it asks for a username and password — the password is **not** your GitHub password but a *token*:
   1. On [github.com](https://github.com): profile photo → **Settings** → bottom of the left sidebar → **Developer settings**.
   2. **Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token → Generate new token (classic)**.
   3. Note: `LEAP hub`. Expiration: **Custom → 2026-12-31**. Scopes: tick the top-level **`repo`** box. Click **Generate token**.
   4. **Copy the token now** — GitHub shows it only once. Treat it like a password: never paste it into a notebook or a file in your repo.

4. **Put your completed notebook in the repo.** Three ways — pick one.

### Option 1 — Upload on the GitHub website

Fine for today; from Lab 1 on we use option 2 or 3.

1. On the hub, right-click `verify_setup.ipynb` in the file browser → **Download**.
2. On your repo's GitHub page: **Add file → Upload files**, drag the file in, click **Commit changes**.

### Option 2 — Using the Terminal

Open a hub terminal (**File → New → Terminal**). Each step is **one command**: run it, read what comes back, then go to the next. If something fails, note which step and see [When git goes wrong](#when-git-goes-wrong).

1. Tell git your name (nothing printed = it worked):
   ```bash
   git config --global user.name "Your Name"
   ```
2. Tell git your email:
   ```bash
   git config --global user.email "your-uni@columbia.edu"
   ```
3. Clear any login setting left over from last week (harmless if there is none):
   ```bash
   git config --global --unset-all credential.helper
   ```
4. Tell git to remember your token after you type it once:
   ```bash
   git config --global credential.helper store
   ```
5. Clone your repo. Because it is private, this asks for a **Username** (your GitHub username) and a **Password** — paste the **token** (nothing appears while you paste; press Enter). A folder `climate-modeling-f26-<uni>` appears in the file browser:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/climate-modeling-f26-<uni>.git
   ```
6. Copy the notebook into that folder:
   ```bash
   cp verify_setup.ipynb climate-modeling-f26-<uni>/
   ```
7. Move into the folder (the prompt changes to show the folder name):
   ```bash
   cd climate-modeling-f26-<uni>
   ```
8. Tell git to track the file:
   ```bash
   git add verify_setup.ipynb
   ```
9. Record a snapshot with a message (git prints a summary like `1 file changed`):
   ```bash
   git commit -m "Lab 0: verification notebook"
   ```
10. Send it to GitHub. This time no password is asked — step 4 remembered the token:
    ```bash
    git push
    ```
11. Reload your repo page on github.com: the notebook should be there.

> **Tried `gh-scoped-creds` last week?** Nothing to redo — your clone uses the same URL. Do steps 1–4, then continue from step 6 inside your existing folder.

### Option 3 — Using the JupyterHub Git interface

Same thing, with buttons. The **Git** panel is in the hub's left sidebar (the branching-arrows icon).

1. Git panel → **Clone a Repository** → paste `https://github.com/<your-username>/climate-modeling-f26-<uni>.git` → OK. It asks for credentials: username, and the **token** as the password.
2. In the file browser, drag `verify_setup.ipynb` into the new `climate-modeling-f26-<uni>` folder, then open that folder.
3. Git panel: the file appears under **Changed**. Click its **+** to stage it, type a message in the box at the bottom, click **Commit**. The first time it asks for your name and email.
4. Click the cloud-up **Push** icon at the top of the panel. If asked, give username + token again.
5. Reload your repo page on github.com: the notebook should be there.

The panel may ask for the token on every push. To stop that, run steps 3–4 of option 2 once in a terminal.

## Part D — Submit your notebook as assignment

On Courseworks, open the **Lab 0** assignment and submit **the URL of your repository** (e.g., `https://github.com/ab1234/climate-modeling-f26-ab1234`). That link-posting step is how every submission works this term: work lives in your repo, the Courseworks link + timestamp is what makes it official.

## When git goes wrong

From Lab 1 on, saving your work to GitHub is the same three commands from inside your repo folder (or the same three clicks in the Git panel — stage, Commit, Push):

1. `git add .` — track everything you changed
2. `git commit -m "what you did"` — record a snapshot
3. `git push` — send it to GitHub

When one of them fails:

| What you see | What it means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Support for password authentication was removed` | You typed your GitHub password | Use the token as the password |
| `Authentication failed` | Wrong username, or a mistyped/expired token | Run `git config --global --unset-all credential.helper`, then push again and re-enter the token; lost the token? generate a new one (Part C, step 3) |
| `Repository not found` (but it exists on github.com) | Typo in the URL | Check `git remote -v` against your repo page |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | You cloned with an `ssh` URL | `git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<user>/<repo>.git` |
| `Updates were rejected because the remote contains work` | The repo changed on the website (e.g. you uploaded a file there) | `git pull`, then `git push` |
| `Please tell me who you are` | Name/email not set | Option 2, steps 1–2 |
| `terminal prompts disabled` | The Git panel could not ask for a password | Run option 2, steps 3–4, then push from the terminal once; after that the panel works |

Still stuck? Ask a TA during the lab or come to office hours. A fuller tour of git on the hub (branches, pulling, resolving conflicts) is in the [LEAP GitHub tutorial](github_tutorial_leap.qmd) — optional.
